 ** Q: can you confirm: when you fit the subject-level models to get the betas, did you estimate them in two separate models, or in one model?**

The subject level models are estimated each with the following formula:

glm(treatment ~ risk.c*gain.c, data = x, family = binomial(link = "logit")

For each subject, I center the risk and gain variables denoted here with “.c” 
Also note that I include the interaction between the two within the model specification.

However. I think I found an issue that does slightly change the betas; mean centering by total sample, rather than by subject

Something principled we can do is exclude subjects with variance inflation factors above some threshold, this would remove subjects from the analysis whose solution is potentially unstable due to the relationship between the risk and gain (i.e. collinearity). 


```{r}

  mutate(gain.c = scale(gain, scale = F)) %>%

  mutate(VAR = (0.5*gain - 0.5*risk)^2) %>%
```

Note we lose 24 subjects that have large VIF and this does not fix our issue of some subjects have the opposite beta values than we would expect.

```{r}
mfxboot <- function(modform,dist,data,boot=1000,digits=3){
  x <- glm(modform, family=binomial(link=dist),data)
  # get marginal effects
  pdf <- ifelse(dist=="probit",
                mean(dnorm(predict(x, type = "link"))),
                mean(dlogis(predict(x, type = "link"))))
  marginal.effects <- pdf*coef(x)
  # start bootstrap
  bootvals <- matrix(rep(NA,boot*length(coef(x))), nrow=boot)
  set.seed(1111)
  for(i in 1:boot){
    samp1 <- data[sample(1:dim(data)[1],replace=T,dim(data)[1]),]
    x1 <- glm(modform, family=binomial(link=dist),samp1)
    pdf1 <- ifelse(dist=="probit",
                   mean(dnorm(predict(x, type = "link"))),
                   mean(dlogis(predict(x, type = "link"))))
    bootvals[i,] <- pdf1*coef(x1)
  }
  res <- cbind(marginal.effects,apply(bootvals,2,sd),marginal.effects/apply(bootvals,2,sd))
  if(names(x$coefficients[1])=="(Intercept)"){
    res1 <- res[2:nrow(res),]
    res2 <- matrix(as.numeric(sprintf(paste("%.",paste(digits,"f",sep=""),sep=""),res1)),nrow=dim(res1)[1])     
    rownames(res2) <- rownames(res1)
    } else {
    res2 <- matrix(as.numeric(sprintf(paste("%.",paste(digits,"f",sep=""),sep="")),nrow=dim(res)[1]))
    rownames(res2) <- rownames(res)
    }
  colnames(res2) <- c("marginal.effect","standard.error","z.score")  
  return(res2)
}

m.marginal <- by(logit.data, logit.data$user_id, function(x) mfxboot(treatment ~ risk.c*gain.c, "logit",data = x, boot=1000 ,digits=7))
```

** Is it the case that in all subjects, they only made judgments about one cognitive function?**
Yes, subjects only made judgments in a one cognitive function. 

So just to show again: testing for the effect of condition on risk and gain
```{r}
x %>% 
  dplyr::select(user_id, condition, CogMotor, marginal.effect.risk, marginal.effect.gain, age, Income, education, conservatismFactor) -> test

aov.risk <- stats::oneway.test(marginal.effect.risk ~ condition, data = test, var.equal= F)
aov.gain <- stats::oneway.test(marginal.effect.gain ~ condition, data = test, var.equal= F)

tab <- map_df(list(aov.risk,aov.gain), tidy)
knitr::kable(tab[c("num.df", "den.df", "statistic", "p.value", "method")], caption = "condition tests")

ggplot(test, 
       aes(x = marginal.effect.risk, 
           fill = condition)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Risk distribution by Condition")

ggplot(test, 
       aes(x = marginal.effect.gain, 
           fill = condition)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Gain distribution by Condition")
```



 **q about the motor condition**
```{r}

t1 <- t.test(marginal.effect.risk ~ CogMotor, test, var.equal=TRUE)
t2 <- t.test(marginal.effect.gain ~ CogMotor, test, var.equal=TRUE)
tab <- map_df(list(t1,t2), tidy)

knitr::kable(tab[c("estimate", "statistic", "p.value", "parameter", "conf.low", 
"conf.high", "method")], caption = "Cog-Motor tests")


ggplot(test, 
       aes(x = marginal.effect.risk, 
           fill = CogMotor)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Risk distribution by Cog-Motor")

ggplot(test, 
       aes(x = marginal.effect.gain, 
           fill = CogMotor)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Gain distribution by Cog-Motor")
```
Here is a t test between cogntive and motor domains for risk and gain. Here we see for gain, a larger gain beta for the motor. So what I could take from this is that in terms of gain, people weight the pros for motor more heaivly than that of cogntive domains. Something I think we could become more sensitive to if we test for this directly. Not sure if it matters here, but I know that the amount of observations in each group could be having an effect. Where because we alot of data for cogntive that variance is lower, and in contrast, motor variance is higher due to low sample amount. 


**In my R01 aims, I'm predicting that "more affluent, educated, liberal, individualist, and younger individuals will be less risk-averse and more benefit-driven." Is this true in our data?**

Note we do not have data of 'individualist' since we choose not to include that measure. 

Below the tables output are each of the linear regression models in order followed by a multivariate model for both risk and gain


```{r data recodeing for demographics}
#Recode the variables for the model
data %>% 
  dplyr::select(user_id, condition, guaussian.risk, guaussian.gain, Risk_Beta, Gain_Beta, Agecat, Incomecat, education, conservatismFactor) %>% 
  mutate(education_recode = fct_recode(education,
  HighSchool = "high school degree",
  Undergraduate = "bachelor",
  Postgraduate = "masters",
  Postgraduate = "Doctoral/Professional"
)) %>% 
  mutate(age_recode = fct_recode(Agecat,
  "18-24" = "(18,24]",
  "25-49" = "(24,49]",
  "50-75" = "(49,75]"
)) %>% 
  mutate(income_recode = fct_recode(Incomecat,
  "< 25,000" = "(0,2.5e+04]",
  "25,000-50,000" = "(2.5e+04,5e+04]",
  "50,000-75,000"= "(5e+04,7.5e+04]",
  "> 75,000" = "(7.5e+04,2e+05]"
)) %>% 
  mutate(educationSUM = C(education_recode, sum)) %>% #then we sum code for the models
  mutate(ageSUM = C(age_recode, sum)) %>% 
  mutate(incomeSUM = C(income_recode, sum)) -> test

#predicting individual differences in risk and gain
lm.1 <- lm(guaussian.risk ~ageSUM, test)
lm.2 <- lm(guaussian.risk ~incomeSUM, test)
lm.3 <- lm(guaussian.risk ~educationSUM, test) 
lm.4 <- lm(guaussian.risk ~conservatismFactor, test)

lm.multi.1 <- lm(guaussian.risk ~ ageSUM + incomeSUM + educationSUM + conservatismFactor, test)

tab <- map_df(list(lm.1,lm.2,lm.3,lm.4, lm.multi.1), tidy)
#%>% filter(!term == "(Intercept)")
knitr::kable(tab[c("term", "estimate", "std.error", "statistic", "p.value")], caption = "risk models")

lm.5 <- lm(guaussian.gain ~ageSUM, test)
lm.6 <- lm(guaussian.gain ~incomeSUM, test)
lm.7 <- lm(guaussian.gain ~educationSUM, test) 
lm.8 <- lm(guaussian.gain ~conservatismFactor, test)

lm.multi.2 <- lm(guaussian.gain ~ ageSUM + incomeSUM + educationSUM + conservatismFactor, test)

tab <- map_df(list(lm.5,lm.6,lm.7,lm.8, lm.multi.2), tidy)
#%>% filter(!term == "(Intercept)")
knitr::kable(tab[c("term", "estimate", "std.error", "statistic", "p.value")], caption = "gain models")
```
This is the opposite effect for conservatism, showing as we increase in conservatism we increase in Risk sensitivity which would mean as you become more conservative, the sensitivity towards risk grows in the positive direction. Yet that would mean that more conservative person would be likly to choose more experimental treatments as risk gets larger.

```{r plots for average gain across grouping}
                width = .1)

ggplot(data=test, aes(x=conservatismFactor, y=guaussian.gain)) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, color = "red") +
        geom_point()
```

**Compute power for a One Factor ANOVA with seven levels**

```{r power analysis,}
#devtools::install_github("arcaldwell49/Superpower")
library(pwr)
library(Superpower) # Daniël Lakens power package
data %>%
  group_by(condition) %>%
  summarize(n = n(),
            mean = mean(Risk_Beta),
            sd = sd(Risk_Beta)) %>% na.omit() -> X

string <- "7b" #7 groups, one for each cog domain
n <- 45 
# Say we are thinking of running 45 people in each condition (this is the average we currently gathered)
mu <- X$mean #extract the Risk_Beta means for each condition
# Enter means in the order that matches the labels below.
sd <- mean(X$sd) #use a single standard deviation to not break the assumption of equal variance
labelnames <- c("condition", "Attention (Concentration)", "Language (spoken)", "Long Term Memory", "Mood", "Motor Function", "Self-control", "Short Term (Working) Memory") #
# the label names should be in the order of the means specified above.
design_result <- ANOVA_design(design = string,
                   n = n,
                   mu = mu,
                   sd = sd,
                   labelnames = labelnames)
alpha_level <- 0.05 #conventional

set.seed(43545)
simulation_result <- ANOVA_power(design_result,
                                 alpha_level = alpha_level,
                                 nsims = 1000,
                                 verbose = FALSE)

exact_result <- ANOVA_exact(design_result,
                            alpha_level = alpha_level,
                            verbose = FALSE)

simulation_result
exact_result

knitr::kable(simulation_result$main_results, caption = "Simulated ANOVA Results")
knitr::kable(exact_result$main_results, caption = "Exact ANOVA Results") 

```
This analysis tells us that running the study with 45 participants in each condition is very likely to not yield a significant test result, even if our expected pattern of differences is true. 

Let’s explore which pattern of means we would need to expect to have 90% power for the ANOVA with 45 participants in each group. 

```{r}
K <- 7
n <- 45
f <- exact_result$main_results$cohen_f
pwr.anova.test(n = n,
               k = K,
               f = f,
               sig.level = alpha_level)$power


K <- 7
n <- 45
sd <- mean(X$sd)
r <- 0
#Calculate f when running simulation
f <- pwr.anova.test(n = n,
                    k = K,
                    power = 0.9,
                    sig.level = alpha_level)$f
f
f2 <- f^2
ES <- f2 / (f2 + 1)
ES
```
So, at least based on Cohen's benchmarks, we have 90% power to detect effects that are slightly below a medium effect benchmark (`f`).
Expressed in eta-squared, we can detect values of `ES` or larger. 

```{r monte carlo, }
monte_result1 <- ANOVA_power(
  design_result,
  alpha_level = 0.05,
  verbose = FALSE,
  emm = TRUE,
  contrast_type = "pairwise",
  emm_p_adjust = "holm",
  nsims = 10000, #set total number of simulations
  seed = 27042020) #set seed for reproducibility

knitr::kable(monte_result1$emm_results[1:2])
```

```{r}
plot_power(design_result, min_n = 10, max_n = 250)


n <- 71
design_result <- ANOVA_design(design = string,
                   n = n, 
                   mu = mu, 
                   sd = sd, 
                   labelnames = labelnames,
                   plot = FALSE) #do not print the plot (same as above)

ANOVA_exact(design_result,
            emm = TRUE)

n <- 150
design_result <- ANOVA_design(design = string,
                   n = n, 
                   mu = mu, 
                   sd = sd, 
                   labelnames = labelnames,
                   plot = FALSE) #do not print the plot (same as above)

ANOVA_exact(design_result,
            emm = TRUE)


monte_result2 <- ANOVA_power(
  design_result,
  alpha_level = 0.05,
  verbose = FALSE,
  emm = TRUE,
  contrast_type = "pairwise",
  emm_p_adjust = "holm",
  nsims = 10000, #set total number of simulations
  seed = 27042020) #set seed for reproducibility

knitr::kable(monte_result1$emm_results[1:2])
```

With 71 participants per condition, power for this simple comparison is varies. If we want to aim for 90% power for follow up tests, we need more participants. 150 participants provides good power for the follow-up comparison between our conditions. But power for the difference between conditions for long-term memory and self control is incredibly low. We would need alot more participants to have 90% power for those comparisons (I did over 100000 subjects per condition, so something is suspect.)


**Note** that this power analyses is bias given that I used the pilot data to make these estimate see citation below for more on that. 



Albers, Casper, and Daniël Lakens. 2018. “When Power Analyses Based on Pilot Data Are Biased: Inaccurate Effect Size Estimators and Follow-up Bias.” Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 74: 187–95. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2017.09.004.


```{r p values}
user_id = names(m.logit) #creates vector of user_id's 
n= nrow(Neuroethics_Judgement)/75
#we want to pull out the models and give them a logical model signficant or not
datalist.pvalue = list()
for (i in user_id){
dat = coef(summary(m.logit[[i]]))[,4]#This is coef pvalues
  datalist.pvalue[[i]] = dat
}
subjectModel.Pvalue <-bind_rows(datalist.pvalue)

colnames(subjectModel.Pvalue) <-  c('Intercept_sig','Risk_sig', 'Gain_sig', 'Interaction_sig')

for (ii in 1:4){
  for(jj in 1:n){
    if (subjectModel.Pvalue[jj,ii] > 0.05)
    subjectModel.Pvalue[jj,ii] <- 0
    else 
      subjectModel.Pvalue[jj,ii] <- 1
  }
}

subjectModel.Pvalue <- cbind.data.frame(user_id, subjectModel.Pvalue[,2:4])
subjectModel.Pvalue$Risk_sig <-  factor(subjectModel.Pvalue$Risk_sig, levels = c(0,1), labels = c("Not Significant","Significant"))
subjectModel.Pvalue$Gain_sig <-  factor(subjectModel.Pvalue$Gain_sig, levels = c(0,1), labels = c("Not Significant","Significant"))
subjectModel.Pvalue$Interaction_sig <-  factor(subjectModel.Pvalue$Interaction_sig, levels = c(0,1), labels = c("Not Significant","Significant"))

library(scales)

plotdata <- subjectModel.Pvalue %>%
  count(Risk_sig) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
         pctlabel = paste0(round(pct*100), "%"))
# plot the bars as percentages, 
# in decending order with bar labels
p1 <- ggplot(plotdata, 
       aes(x = reorder(Risk_sig, -pct),
           y = pct)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", 
           fill = "indianred3", 
           color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = pctlabel), 
            vjust = -0.25) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), 
            vjust=-3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, breaks=seq(0,1,.10), limits=c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Risk", 
       y = "Percent", 
       title  = "Participants by P values")


plotdata <- subjectModel.Pvalue %>%
  count(Gain_sig) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n),
         pctlabel = paste0(round(pct*100), "%"))


p2 <- ggplot(plotdata, 
       aes(x = reorder(Gain_sig, -pct),
           y = pct)) + 
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", 
           fill = "indianred3", 
           color = "black") +
  geom_text(aes(label = pctlabel), 
            vjust = -0.25) +
   geom_text(aes(label = n), 
            vjust=-3) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent, breaks=seq(0,1,.10), limits=c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Gain", 
       y = "Percent", 
       title  = "Betas by P values")

plotdata <- subjectModel.Pvalue %>%
  count(Interaction_sig) %>%
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n),

p3 <- ggplot(plotdata,
```
